---
title: "Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics"
---

DeCovarT needs **one sparse Gaussian graphical model per cell type at
the population (pseudo-bulk) level**, not a per-cell precision and not a
directed regulatory DAG. The estimand, aligned with the article, is

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}
\equiv
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}
\ \text{sparse},
$$ {#eq-grn-estimand}

with undirected edges encoding conditional dependence
[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008; @mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011].
Single-cell UMI profiles are the **only observations**. They are **not**
the objects that enter the deconvolution likelihood: we use them to
**estimate** $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j})$ for labelled
types in the Suppinger murine gastruloid resource
[@suppingerMultimodalCharacterizationMurine2023]. Downstream, those
parameters discriminate types via mean shifts **and** precision rewiring,
then enter the convolution

$$
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}
\mid
(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\!\bigl(
\boldsymbol{\mu}\,\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\,
\textstyle\sum_{j}p_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
\bigr).
$$ {#eq-grn-convolution}

Some DeCovarT vignettes write $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ for the same
precision; we keep $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ as in the article Methods.

## Scope of the core pipeline {#sec-grn-scope}

**In scope:** undirected GGMs; single-cell **transcriptomics only**;
**stationarity** (no RNA velocity, no time-varying graphs); labelled
cell types (Suppinger annotations), not unsupervised clustering of the
graph.

**Out of scope for the core, relocated to @sec-grn-appendix:**
multi-omics (ATAC, ChIP, spatial); causal DAGs; temporal dynamics;
fused / joint graphs across types; copula constructions such as JGCGM
that go beyond a Gaussian or Poisson-lognormal observation model.

**Dataset constraint.** GSE229513 is a 10x Chromium 3′ v3 UMI resource
with **one** technical scRNA-seq experiment, not independent biological
replicates for GRNs. GSE250136 is a later stem-embryo dataset; it is
external validation, not extra Suppinger replicates. Technical bootstrap
of cells is allowed (@sec-align-bootstrap); biological bootstrap is not.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-grn-core
%%| fig-cap: "Core route from labelled UMI counts to DeCovarT population Gaussians. Observation processing is method-conditional, not a free factorial arm. Joint and copula estimators sit in the appendix."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone"}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["UMI counts, labels j"] --> B["Gene panel G"]
  B --> C{"Does the estimator assume Gaussian observations?"}
  C -->|yes: SILGGM, low-rank GGM, GmGM copula| D["NPN or depth residuals, then GGM"]
  C -->|no: PLN / PLNFGL| E["Raw counts, latent Gaussian"]
  D --> F["Sparse Theta_j, SPD"]
  E --> F
  F --> G["Type-level pseudo-bulk moments"]
  G --> H["DeCovarT mu_j, Sigma_j"]
  B -.-> I["Appendix: FGL, JGCGM"]
```

## Observation processing is method-conditional {#sec-grn-observation}

The first pipeline put `SCTransform` and `huge::huge.npn()` on the
**same Cartesian axis** as the graph estimator. That is the wrong
product. A transformation is part of the **observation model of a given
estimator**, not an innocent preprocessing step that can be crossed with
every GRN method.

| Estimator family | Observation | Latent object for DeCovarT |
|------------------|-------------|----------------------------|
| `SILGGM` / glasso / sparse+low-rank GGM | Continuous Gaussian (after NPN or, at most, as a sensitivity, Pearson residuals) | $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ on that Gaussian scale |
| `GmGM` | Gaussian copula / nonparanormal on the matrix | gene-axis precision (and a cell-axis precision we do not export) |
| `PLNmodels` / PLNFGL | **Raw UMI counts** | precision of the **latent** log-normal Gaussian |
| Directed ZINB DAGs | Counts with a structural-zero layer | **not** a DeCovarT precision (@nte-drop-zico) |

If the method assumes a Gaussian vector, Gaussianise **inside that
method**. If the method is a Poisson-lognormal hierarchical model, pass
counts. Do **not** run `SCTransform` and then `PLNnetwork`: the PLN
already has a Poisson sampling layer. Do **not** treat NPN as a global
default (the improved pipeline is explicit that applying the ordinary
nonparanormal map directly to counts can be problematic; JGCGM was
written to avoid that).

The three `huge.npn` modes remain relevant **only** for the Gaussian
branch [@liuNonparanormalSemiparametricEstimation2009; @R-huge]:

| `npn.func` | Returns | Use with `SILGGM` |
|------------|---------|-------------------|
| `shrinkage` | $n\times G$ inverse-normal scores | Default Gaussianisation |
| `truncation` | $n\times G$ winsorised scores | Heavy tails |
| `skeptic` | $G\times G$ **correlation** (rank copula; [arXiv:1202.2169](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.2169)) | **Not** a drop-in `SILGGM` data matrix |

`SCTransform` Pearson residuals [@hafemeisterNormalizationVarianceStabilization2019]
stay in the **HVG ranking** of @sec-fs-hvg. Using them as the GGM table
is a sensitivity arm, not a factorial factor.

::: {#nte-npn-moments .callout-warning}
## :warning: Nonparanormal maps are not affine, so they break moments

`huge::huge.npn()` replaces each margin by a (truncated or shrunk)
inverse-normal score
[@liuNonparanormalSemiparametricEstimation2009]. That map $\varphi$ is
**monotone but not affine**. Jensen's inequality then says
$\varphi(\mathbb{E}[y_{g}])\neq\mathbb{E}[\varphi(y_{g})]$ unless the
margin is degenerate (@nte-jensen-transform). A glasso fitted after NPN
therefore targets the precision of a **different random vector** than
the population Gaussian DeCovarT convolves. Use NPN only **inside** the
SILGGM / Gaussian branch, never as a global preprocessing of counts,
and never export NPN-scale means as $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$.
:::

::: {#nte-jensen-transform .callout-important}
## :warning: Transforming the response is usually the wrong GLM

DeCovarT's mean map $\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}$ is **additive on
the measurement scale of $\boldsymbol{y}$**. Replacing $\boldsymbol{y}$ by
$\varphi(\boldsymbol{y})$ and then treating the transform as Gaussian does
three separate kinds of damage.

**1. Jensen: moments of $\varphi(\boldsymbol{y})$ are not $\varphi$ of the
moments.** For a convex $\varphi$, the probabilistic form of Jensen's
inequality states
$\varphi(\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}])\le\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\boldsymbol{y})]$, with
equality iff $\boldsymbol{y}$ is almost surely constant or $\varphi$ is
affine
([Wikipedia, probabilistic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jensen%27s_inequality#Probabilistic_form)).
The logarithm is **concave**, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[\log y_{g}]
\le
\log\mathbb{E}[y_{g}],
$$ {#eq-jensen-log}

and $\log1p$ is likewise concave on $[0,\infty)$. A glasso fitted to
$\log1p$ counts therefore targets a precision of a **different random
vector**. The mean of the transformed table is not the transform of the
mean that DeCovarT needs in @eq-grn-convolution, and the covariance is
not the delta-method image of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$ unless one
explicitly builds that expansion and lives with its bias. Population
aggregation (@sec-align-invariance) compounds the error: the sum of
transformed cells is not the transform of the sum.

**2. The estimand of a transformed linear model is not the estimand of
the original mean.** In a Gaussian linear model,
$\mathbb{E}[\log y\mid x]=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x$ describes
**multiplicative** effects on $y$ after exponentiation, not additive
shifts of $\mathbb{E}[y\mid x]$
([University of Virginia Library, interpreting log transformations](https://library.virginia.edu/data/articles/interpreting-log-transformations-in-a-linear-model)).
Coefficient recipes ($e^{\hat\beta}-1$ as a percent change, and the
log–log elasticity case) are coherent **only** if that multiplicative
model is the scientific target. DeCovarT's target is a **linear
mixture of means** plus a quadratic mixture of covariances. Percent
changes on a log scale do not plug into
$\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}$ or $\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$.

**3. A GLM with the right mean–variance function is preferable to
transforming $y$.** Transforming the response to force Gaussianity,
homoscedasticity, or linearity is a classical but brittle habit: it
changes the parameter, complicates residuals, and still fails when the
mean–variance relationship is mean-dependent (count overdispersion).
The constructive alternative is a generalised linear (or hierarchical)
model on the original $y$ — here, Poisson-lognormal or
negative-binomial sampling with a latent Gaussian — rather than
`log1p` followed by glasso. That is the content of Olszewski's
argument against transforming the response in regression
([LinkedIn article](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/why-transforming-response-regression-analysis-testing-olszewski/);
[activity permalink](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7503551786855649280/)):
test the mean–variance assumption; if it fails, change the **model**,
not the **measurement**.

**Consequence for this book.** Variance-stabilising maps belong in HVG
ranking and, when a method *literally* requires Gaussian rows, as a
**method-specific** Gaussianisation. They are not a third axis of the
benchmark. The improved pipeline's factorial

$$
\text{observation model}
\times
\text{precision estimator}
\times
\text{cross-type sharing}
$$

collapses the first factor to: **Gaussianised input if and only if the
estimator is a Gaussian GGM; raw counts if the estimator is PLN**.
Cross-type sharing is appendix (@sec-grn-appendix).
:::

## Core comparators {#sec-grn-core}

Four families respect the core constraints (undirected, stationary,
transcriptomics-only, exportable as a sparse SPD
$\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ or as a latent Gaussian precision). We compare
them on assumptions versus @eq-grn-estimand, not on unpublished
accuracy numbers.

### `SILGGM`: five inferential modes, one generative precision {#sec-silggm}

`SILGGM` is a frequentist toolkit for high-dimensional GGMs
[@zhangSILGGMExtensivePackage2018; @R-SILGGM]. After optional NPN, it
takes an $n\times G$ table and estimates $\theta_{gg'}$ (or
de-sparsified versions) with four inferential procedures, the last of
which has two penalty flavours:

| Mode | What is computed | Role |
|------|------------------|------|
| `B_NW_SL` | Bivariate nodewise scaled lasso | Edge-wise $\hat\theta_{gg'}$, CIs, $p$-values |
| `D-S_NW_SL` | De-sparsified nodewise scaled lasso | Debiased nodewise edges, CIs |
| `D-S_GL` | De-sparsified graphical lasso | Debiased glasso edges, CIs |
| `GFC_SL` | GGM estimation with FDR, scaled lasso | Simultaneous tests of all pairs |
| `GFC_L` | Same with lasso (tuning for FDR) | Preferred when $n$ is small |

All five share two steps: a lasso-type regularisation (graphical lasso
or $O(G)$ nodewise regressions), then $(G^{2}-G)/2$ asymptotically
normal statistics under a sparsity condition on the maximum degree.
`global=TRUE` extends the first three modes to the GFC FDR framework.
Outputs include estimators, $z$-scores, $p$-values, and (for global
mode) adjacency matrices at a target FDR.

**What the first pipeline got wrong.**

1.  **D-S_GL is not universally preferred.** The SILGGM simulations
    report that `B_NW_SL` and `D-S_NW_SL` can give better
    confidence-interval behaviour for *non-zero* partial correlations
    than `D-S_GL`. For a small gene set that needs CIs, `B_NW_SL` is
    the authors' own recommendation; `D-S_NW_SL` is the cheaper
    alternative at $G\sim 10^{4}$. For whole-graph FDR, `GFC_L` is
    recommended when $n$ is small (order $10^{2}$) because tuning
    helps FDR; at larger $n$ the four modes are similar.
2.  **The de-sparsified formula is not $2\hat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}-S$.**
    The Janková–van de Geer estimator is
    $\widehat{T}=2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}\widehat{R}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}$
    with $\widehat{R}$ the empirical correlation
    [@jankovaConfidenceIntervalsHighdimensional2015]. The first
    report's $2\hat\Theta-S$ is incorrect.
3.  **The debiased matrix is deliberately non-sparse.** It is built for
    inference, not as a generative precision. Feeding $\widehat{T}$ to
    DeCovarT would export a dense, not necessarily well-conditioned,
    $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$. The statistically clean composition
    (**proposal**) is: use debiasing / FDR to **select a support**,
    then re-estimate a positive-definite precision *on that support*
    (constrained MLE when the graph is chordal; otherwise a constrained
    glasso or a small ridge). That separates **edge testing** from the
    **SPD object** in @eq-grn-estimand.

**Pros.** Fast C++ implementation; $p$-values and FDR; scales to
thousands of genes; matches the undirected GGM language of DeCovarT;
CRAN package.

**Cons.** Gaussian observations (NPN is a copula patch, not a count
model); no dropout / library-size layer; independent cells; independent
types (no pooling); debiased estimators are the wrong generative object;
on UMI data the authors themselves used $\log_{2}(\mathrm{UMI}+1)$
then NPN — which is exactly the transform @nte-jensen-transform
criticises. That said, Zhang and Zou
[@zhangSparsePrecisionMatrix2014] report that the graphical lasso
estimator of a sparse precision is usually still **support-consistent**:
it recovers the zeros of the true direct (conditional) interactions even
when the multivariate Gaussian assumption does not hold. That is
reassurance for **edge screening**, not a licence to treat the glasso
point estimate as the DeCovarT generative $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$. We
keep `SILGGM` as a **benchmark branch**, not as “the” pipeline, and we
prefer `GFC_L` / glasso **support** plus an SPD refit over exporting
`D-S_GL` point estimates.

It does **not** model unknown mixtures: subset cells by annotation
first. A Bayesian latent mixture with dropout (`BLGGM`) is **not** in
the $4\times 3\times 2$ product: labels are already known, and MCMC
plus a gene cap of a few hundred make it a perspective only.

### Poisson-lognormal: Chiquet's `PLNmodels` versus PLNFGL {#sec-pln}

Two PLN estimators share Aitchison and Ho's hierarchical construction
and **differ** in how they estimate $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$.

**Observation model (common).** For cell $c$ of type $j$, library
size $S_{c}$, latent intensities $\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}$,

$$
Y_{cg}\mid\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathrm{Poisson}(S_{c}Z_{cg}),
\qquad
\log\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}.
$$ {#eq-pln}

Zeros are sampling zeros under a Poisson with random log-normal mean;
a separate structural-zero (ZINB) layer is not required
[@chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021]. That matches Svensson's
critique of automatic zero-inflation for droplet UMI data
[@svenssonDropletScRNAseqNot2020].

**Chiquet: variational sparse PLN (`PLNnetwork`).** The `PLNmodels`
framework [@R-PLNmodels] treats the PLN as a versatile count GGM and
estimates a sparse latent precision by variational inference with an
$\ell_{1}$ penalty on $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$
[@chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021;
@chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018]. Later work in the same group
studies zero-inflation **inside** the PLN family as an extension, not as
the default [@batardiereZeroInflationMultivariatePoisson2025]. The
exported object is exactly a latent Gaussian precision — the DeCovarT
estimand — with a sampling model that respects UMI counts. Fits are
typically **per condition** unless one stacks a group penalty by hand.

**Zhai et al. PLNFGL (2026).** PLNFGL estimates a moment covariance for
the latent Gaussian and plugs it into the **fused graphical lasso** of
Danaher, Wang and Witten: within-type $\ell_{1}$ sparsity plus a fusion
penalty that shrinks $\theta_{gg'}^{(j)}$ towards
$\theta_{gg'}^{(\ell)}$ across conditions
[@zhaiPLNFGLJointEstimation2026; @danaherJointGraphicalLasso2012]. That
is joint estimation. It belongs in @sec-grn-appendix as a sharing
strategy, not in the core independent-type comparison. It is nonetheless
the closest **published** composition to “PLN observations + several
related $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$”.

| | Chiquet `PLNnetwork` | PLNFGL (Zhai) |
|--|----------------------|----------------|
| Sampling | PLN | PLN |
| $\Sigma$ | Variational likelihood | Moments + PD projection |
| $\Theta$ | $\ell_{1}$ on one graph | Fused glasso, $J$ graphs |
| Sharing across types | No (unless redesigned) | Yes ($\lambda_{2}$) |
| Core vs appendix | **Core** | Appendix |

**Pros of the PLN family.** Count likelihood; latent Gaussian precision
is the DeCovarT object; no obligatory NPN; library size $S_{c}$ is
explicit; fusion (PLNFGL) is available when we *choose* to pool.

**Cons.** Moment estimators of $\Sigma$ can be crude in $G\gg n$;
variational PLN is heavier than glasso; fusion can **erase** the
rewiring DeCovarT wants if $\lambda_{2}$ is large; none of these
methods gives SILGGM-style edgewise FDR out of the box.

**Critical recommendation.** Cite Chiquet for the PLN **model and
variational sparse precision**, and Zhai for **moments + fusion**. On
Suppinger, the core PLN arm is **Chiquet `PLNnetwork` per labelled
type**. PLNFGL is the fused extension.

### Multi-axis GGMs (`GmGM`): cells are not independent rows {#sec-gmgm}

Almost every GGM above makes the **independence assumption**: to learn
the gene precision, cells are i.i.d. rows. That is false in a gastruloid
— cells share a microenvironment, a lineage, and (in spatial assays)
neighbours. `GmGM` [@andrewMakingMultiaxisGaussian2026] replaces
independence with a **Cartesian
product** assumption: gene $g$ in cell $c$ may depend on other genes
in the same cell, or on the same gene in other cells, but not on
arbitrary cell–gene pairs. The precision of $\mathrm{vec}(X)$ is a
Kronecker **sum** of a gene precision and a cell precision. A Gaussian
copula (nonparanormal) weakens Gaussian margins. The 2026 contribution
is scalability to millions of cells via a low-rank / linearly sparse
eigendecomposition; the Python package is `GmGM`.

**Pros.** Direct stress test of the i.i.d.-cell assumption that
underwrites both SILGGM and the aggregation algebra in
@sec-align-invariance; jointly estimates a cell graph (lineage /
communication proxy) and a gene graph; copula margins.

**Cons.** The statistical object is **not** @eq-grn-estimand: one gene
precision is shared across cells, with residual dependence pushed into
the cell axis. DeCovarT wants **type-specific**
$\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$, which requires subsetting types *or*
interpreting the cell graph as a substitute for type labels. Kronecker
structure is a modelling restriction. Multi-omics shared-axis examples
in the paper (RNA+ATAC) are out of our core scope.

**Use.** External stress test, not the default DeCovarT estimator. If
the gene-axis precision on a type subset disagrees violently with
per-type SILGGM / PLN, the i.i.d. assumption is a suspect.

### Sparse plus low-rank latent-variable GGMs {#sec-lowrank}

A sparse GGM assumes that, after conditioning on the observed genes,
the remaining dependence is sparse. Unmeasured programmes — cell cycle,
maturation, sequencing depth not captured by a size factor — induce a
**dense** marginal precision. Chandrasekaran, Parrilo and Willsky
separate a sparse conditional interaction matrix among observed genes
from a **low-rank** contribution of latent factors
[@chandrasekaranLatentVariableGraphical2012]:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathrm{marg}}
=
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathrm{sparse}}
-
\boldsymbol{L},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{L}\succeq 0,\
\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{L})\ll G.
$$ {#eq-slr}

**Pros.** Protects the gene graph against global confounders that are
rampant in scRNA-seq; the sparse summand is the object one would like
to call “regulation”; conceptually close to factor-adjusted GGMs.

**Cons.** Identifiability needs incoherence between the sparse and
low-rank parts; tuning two penalties; the low-rank piece is **not** a
DeCovarT type covariance — it is a nuisance. If the sparse component
changes dramatically relative to ordinary glasso, inferred edges may
have been global programmes.

**Use.** Robustness experiment on the same gene panel as SILGGM. If
sparse edges are stable, ordinary glasso was not merely fitting cell
cycle; if they collapse, do not export the dense glasso to DeCovarT.

## Four methods to carry forward {#sec-grn-top4}

Given stationarity, a multivariate Gaussian **population** object,
sparsity, and single-cell transcriptomics only, the four most
defensible **core** routes are:

1.  **`SILGGM` `GFC_L` (or glasso) → FDR support → SPD refit**, with
    NPN **inside this branch only**. Inferential, scalable, closest in
    language to the article's gLasso precision
    [@mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011; @zhangSILGGMExtensivePackage2018].
2.  **Chiquet `PLNnetwork` per labelled type.** Count-honest latent
    Gaussian; no NPN; library size explicit
    [@chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021].
3.  **Sparse + low-rank GGM** on the Gaussianised (or copula) scale.
    Confounder check before trusting $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$.
4.  **`GmGM` on type subsets** as a multi-axis stress test of
    independent cells — interpret the **gene-axis** precision, do not
    force the cell-axis precision into DeCovarT.

PLNFGL, joint graphical lasso, and JGCGM are **sharing** strategies
(@sec-grn-appendix). They may well beat independent fits on variance,
but they risk shrinking away the rewiring that is the scientific target.
`SCENIC` / `GRNBoost2` [@aibarScenicSinglecellRegulatory2017;
@moermanGRNBoost2ArboretoEfficient2019] are directed, TF-centred
boosting methods: valuable as **knowledge-driven baselines** in
@sec-metrics-knowledge, not as DeCovarT precisions.

Every core method must finally export the same object

$$
\bigl\{
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j}
\bigr\}_{j=1}^{J},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}^{-1}
\succ 0.
$$ {#eq-grn-export}

::: {#nte-drop-zico .callout-warning}
## :warning: Why we drop zero-inflated directed graphs in the core

Directed zero-inflated DAGs (for example
[arXiv:2512.16233](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16233)) are the wrong
object for DeCovarT: the output is a DAG, not an undirected SPD
precision; projecting to a skeleton discards the Gaussian convolution
that the likelihood needs.

There is a deeper sampling reason not to *start* from ZINB at all on
this dataset. Suppinger is **droplet UMI** 10x data. Svensson showed
that zeros in droplet scRNA-seq are often explained by ordinary
molecule-sampling count distributions
[@svenssonDropletScRNAseqNot2020]. Automatic zero-inflation is then
unidentifiable and scientifically unmotivated.

Keep hurdle / ZINB graphs in the sensitivity chapter
(@sec-sensitivity) if we want to contaminate the observation model, not
as a GRN estimator.
:::

## Revised design product {#sec-grn-design}

The improved pipeline's three-way factorial is right in spirit and wrong
in its first factor. The product we will actually interpret is
(@fig-pipeline)

$$
\underbrace{\{\text{SILGGM+NPN},\ \text{PLN counts},\ \text{sparse+low-rank},\ \text{GmGM}\}}_{\text{four GGM families}}
\times
\underbrace{\{\text{affine},\ \text{Bures--Wasserstein},\ \text{scDesign2}\}}_{\text{three population lifts}}
\times
\underbrace{\{\mathcal{G}_{0},\ \text{optional NSGA-II}\}}_{\text{two panels}}.
$$ {#eq-grn-product}

That is up to 24 routes. Independent type-level fits are the **core**
sharing strategy; fused / copula-joint sharing stays in
@sec-grn-appendix. `SCTransform` and `huge.npn` are **not** crossed with
PLN. `BLGGM` is not in the product.

Scripts (when implemented): `scripts/03_01_grn_silggm.R` and a PLN
script still to be added. No code is given here.

## Appendix: sharing and copulas {#sec-grn-appendix}

### Fused and joint graphical lasso

Related gastruloid types should share part of their graph and differ on
a sparse rewiring set. The joint graphical lasso
[@danaherJointGraphicalLasso2012] estimates
$\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{J}$ together with a group
or fused penalty. **PLNFGL** is the PLN observation layer plus fused
glasso [@zhaiPLNFGLJointEstimation2026].

The modelling decision — independent versus partially pooled precisions
— is more consequential than glasso versus nodewise lasso. For DeCovarT
the risk is shrinkage of $\Delta_{j\ell}$. If fusion is used, keep
$\lambda_{2}$ small and compare supports to the independent SILGGM /
PLN fits. Full joint estimation is **not** the core default until we
can show that rewiring of developmental neighbours is preserved.

### Gaussian copulas beyond NPN: JGCGM

JGCGM learns several subgroup networks from scRNA-seq with a Gaussian
copula and an explicit split between shared and subgroup-specific
edges [@wuJointLearningMultiple2020]. The authors warn against naïve
NPN on counts. That is the right warning; the method is still a
**copula GGM**, hence undirected and stationary, but it is a joint
estimator (appendix) and it does not provide a PLN sampling layer. Use
it as a copula-aware fused comparator if an implementation is
available; do not replace PLN on UMI counts without a benchmark.

Chiquet's earlier work on latent organisation, sample heterogeneity,
time-course, and multi-attribute GGMs (HDR; SIMoNe; cooperative lasso)
supplies **structured penalties**
[@chiquetSparsitySigncoherentGroups2012] that could encode pathway
modules. Those penalties are optional regularisers, not a second
estimand.
